titleEn: Sing to Him a new song
progression: | C C | G G | Am F | C G |
intro: Twenty-two verses, one for each letter of the alphabet, though the psalm is not an acrostic, and one of the few psalms in the first book of Tehilim with no heading at all: it opens on a plural imperative and never names an author. Said on Shabbat and festival mornings among the psalms of praise that come before the Shema. The thing to watch is verses 10 and 11: the same two nouns, counsel and plans, are used first of the nations and then of God, and the second use cancels the first.

stichs.en: Sing for joy in the LORD, you righteous;
praise is fitting for the upright.

verses.summary: The psalm opens on a plural imperative with no speaker named. Praise is called fitting for the upright, which makes the singing a question of fit rather than of mood.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the LORD with the lyre,
make music to Him on the ten-stringed harp.

verses.summary: Instruments arrive in the second line before any content of the praise is given. Whatever this praise is, it is public and scored, not private.

stichs.en: Sing Him a new song,
play well, with a shout of joy.

verses.summary: Novelty and craft are asked for in the same line: a new song, played skilfully. The shout at the end is the same word used for a horn blast at a festival.

stichs.en: For the word of the LORD is upright,
and all His work is done in faithfulness.

verses.summary: The reason for the singing arrives. It is a claim about character, word and work, before any single act of God has been named.

stichs.en: He loves righteousness and justice;
the earth is full of the LORD's steadfast love.

verses.summary: Justice is what He loves; kindness is what the ground under the singer is already full of. The second half says something about the world, not about the worshipper.

stichs.en: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made,
and by the breath of His mouth all their host.

verses.summary: Creation by speech and by breath, with no craft and no struggle. The host of heaven, the whole array of stars, arrives as the by-product of an exhalation.

stichs.en: He gathers the waters of the sea like a heap,
He puts the deeps in storehouses.

verses.summary: Two participles keep the action open: gathering, putting. The sea is handled like stock in a warehouse, which is a quiet joke at the expense of the sea's reputation.

stichs.en: Let all the earth fear the LORD;
let all who live in the world stand in awe of Him.

verses.summary: The conclusion drawn from creation is fear, not applause. Two verbs of dread balance the two words for the inhabited world.

stichs.en: For He spoke, and it came to be;
He commanded, and it stood firm.

verses.summary: The shortest verse in the psalm and the hinge of its argument. Speech and result are separated by nothing but a conjunction.

stichs.en: The LORD annuls the counsel of the nations,
He thwarts the plans of the peoples.

verses.summary: The power that made the heavens is turned on politics. Two verbs of cancellation, one for the counsel of the nations and one for their plans.

stichs.en: The counsel of the LORD stands forever,
the plans of His heart for generation after generation.

verses.summary: The mirror of verse 10, noun for noun. The verb that made creation stand firm in verse 9 is the verb used here for policy.

stichs.en: Happy is the nation whose God is the LORD,
the people He chose as His own inheritance.

verses.summary: The word for nation here is the same one used for the foreign nations two verses earlier. What separates this nation is not its counsel but its being chosen.

stichs.en: From heaven the LORD looks down,
He sees all the children of Adam.

verses.summary: The angle changes. After eight verses of a God who speaks, here is a God who looks, and what He takes in is all of humanity at once.

stichs.en: From the place where He sits He gazes
on all the inhabitants of the earth.

verses.summary: The looking gets a location and an intensity. The verb is stronger than the one in verse 13: a fixed, deliberate watching rather than a glance.

stichs.en: He who forms the hearts of them all,
who discerns all their deeds.

verses.summary: He formed the hearts He is now reading. This is why the watching of verses 13 and 14 is not treated as surveillance from outside.

stichs.en: No king is saved by a large army,
no warrior is rescued by great strength.

verses.summary: The turn to the practical, and both examples are put in the passive: the king is not saved, the warrior is not rescued, and no rescuer is named.

stichs.en: The horse is a false hope for victory,
and its great strength brings no escape.

verses.summary: The horse was the heavy armour of the ancient Near East. Calling it a lie is a technical claim about where rescue comes from, not a complaint about cavalry.

stichs.en: The eye of the LORD is on those who fear Him,
on those who wait for His steadfast love.

verses.summary: The counter-image to the horse. An eye rather than an army, turned toward two groups that turn out to be one: those who fear and those who wait.

stichs.en: to rescue their soul from death,
and to keep them alive in famine.

verses.summary: What the eye is for. Death and famine are precisely the two things a king with a large army cannot stop, which is the pair verses 16 and 17 dismissed.

stichs.en: Our soul waits for the LORD;
He is our help and our shield.

verses.summary: The congregation takes over. Until now the psalm spoke about people in the third person; from here it says our, and it keeps saying it to the end.

stichs.en: For our heart rejoices in Him,
because we have trusted in His holy name.

verses.summary: Joy and trust in one breath, with the trust given as the cause of the joy. The holy name now occupies the place the horse and the army held.

stichs.en: Let Your steadfast love, LORD, be upon us,
just as we have waited for You.

verses.summary: The one request in twenty-two verses, and it asks for nothing new. It asks that the kindness of verse 5, which already fills the earth, land here.

pardes.body: The psalm is built in blocks. Verses 1 to 3 are the call, all imperatives and instruments. Verses 4 and 5 give the reason in a single sentence about word and work. Verses 6 to 9 are creation by speech, closing on the two clauses of verse 9. Verses 10 to 12 apply that speech to history, where what the nations decide gets cancelled. Verses 13 to 15 turn the same God into an observer. Verses 16 to 19 dismiss military power and put an eye where the army was, and verses 20 to 22 answer in the first person plural. The spine is a single verb: {{9.6}}, what stood at creation, and {{11.3}}, what stands in counsel, are the same root.

Verses 10 and 11 use the same two nouns in the same order. {{10.2}}, the counsel of the nations, is broken; {{11.0}}, the counsel of the LORD, stands. The plans of the peoples and the plans of His heart follow the same pattern. Nothing in the vocabulary marks the second pair as superior, only the verbs do. In verse 7 the word {{7.1}}, a heap, is the noun used of the sea standing up at the crossing in Exodus 15:8. The Septuagint read the consonants as a different word and translated a wineskin instead, so in Greek God pours the sea into a container rather than piling it up. Both readings are ancient and the choice between them is still argued.

Verse 15 is the proof text in Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2 for the image of the new year as a review: all who enter the world pass before Him like bnei maron, a phrase the Talmud then has to explain, and the verse is quoted to say that the one who forms their hearts together considers all their deeds. The whole reading hangs on {{15.1}}: it can mean that He forms all hearts at once, or that He forms them alike, or that He takes them in together in one act, and the liturgy depends on the last sense. Verse 6 does separate work. Avot 5:1 counts ten utterances of creation, but Genesis 1 has only nine explicit sayings, and the Talmud supplies the tenth from this verse, reading the first word of the Torah as an utterance in its own right.

The kabbalistic reading takes verse 6 apart into two channels. The word makes the heavens, the breath of the mouth makes their host, so speech and breath become two grades of one act, the first giving structure and the second giving animation. The ten utterances of Avot are identified in this literature with the ten sefirot, which turns {{6.0}} from a report about a past moment into a description of continuous emanation: heaven is not made once, it is being spoken. The three appearances of kindness in the psalm, {{5.3}} filling the world, {{18.6}} reaching those who wait, and {{22.1}} in the closing request, are read as one flow measured at three points, so the last verse asks only that what already fills the earth be received here.
